segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Twenty-two children come now. Nine more from the mill cottages, if the lane were passable in February.

segments.speaker: Miss Louisa Marchmont
segments.text: Twenty-two. And a roof that wants fifteen pounds and has nine shillings.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Mr Rowe stands under the crack when he reads to them, so that whatever comes away comes away on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Miss Marchmont took the lantern out of the maid's hand and went off across the glebe without waiting for the road. She began her letter to her uncle that night. By Friday she had not finished it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Bramdean errand was Mrs Pike's arrangement. Fenner the mason would set no figure on paper for a man who had not stood in his yard, and Bramdean is six miles. Mr Rowe had the loan of the Ludds' donkey cart on the Friday.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Six miles out and six back, and nothing to do the whole way but talk. I have never known it fail.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the Friday morning the gatehouse maid came down with a note. Miss Marchmont was at her fourth sheet to her uncle and could not go to Bramdean until the post went out on Tuesday.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Pike read it on her own doorstep with the cart already at the gate. Miss Vane came across the green at that moment, going up to the draper's for black thread.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Miss Vane. You are walking anyway. Go with him and see the figure written down and the man's name under it, for the curate will come home with the sum in his head and lose the shillings out of it.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I am going for thread.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Thread will keep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It did not occur to her, then or for some hours afterwards, that there was nobody in the cart but the two of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A mile past the mill the near wheel split from the spoke outward, and the cart sat down on its axle. Rowe tied the donkey to the hedge. There was nothing to do but wait for somebody to come along the road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They sat on the verge. It was a quarter of an hour before either of them said anything that was not about the wheel.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: It was Chronicles.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: It was.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I have carried that morning about with me since January. In my account of it there were six people in the room, and one of the Barrow girls laughed.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: There were four of us and nobody laughed. You had said it twice already, and you were going to the visitation on the Thursday. I thought it kinder to say it in front of Mrs Hale than to let you say it in front of the archdeacon.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I did not take it for kindness at the time.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I wrote out a list of six books in February. It came back into my hand on the green, and you had not read one of them.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I had not. I was ashamed of the word I used before I reached the lych gate, and I have never said so aloud until this minute.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Trash.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Trash. And Nan Corbin lay there till the summer with nothing to look at but a ceiling.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith looked at the road, which stayed empty. In her own account he had smiled while he said it. He had not smiled. She had put the smile in herself, because it made the thing easier to hold.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: We have neither of us been telling it straight.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: No. Mine had grown a good deal in the keeping.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was the better part of an hour before Nye came by with a load of hurdles and room for two on the board. The sun was well down before the first cottages showed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith was laughing as they came in, at something he had said about Fenner's yard dog, and she was laughing still when they came round the corner of the green.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The green was not empty. It was Friday. The London coach stood outside the Bell with its lamps lit and half the parish about it. Above the draper's the library window was bright, and Mrs Hale stood in it.
